paths.title: Responsive Design & Adaptive Interfaces
paths.description: Build interfaces that adapt to viewport, container, input, motion, zoom, safe areas, and content rather than targeting a few device widths.
topics: Mobile-first composition
A narrow-screen baseline forces prioritization and avoids depending on desktop space that may not exist.
Start with a usable compact layout and add enhancements when content or component constraints justify them.
Content-driven breakpoints
Breakpoints should respond to layout failure or opportunity rather than named device models.
Resize with real content and add a breakpoint where relationships become crowded, unreadable, or unnecessarily sparse.
Container-based adaptation
Components often need to adapt to their allocated width even when viewport size is unchanged.
Use container queries for reusable panels and reserve viewport media queries for application-level environmental changes.
Responsive typography
Readable type scales with available space while retaining usable minimum and maximum sizes.
Use relative units and clamp-based ranges, then test zoom, text scaling, and long translated strings.
Responsive images
srcset, sizes, picture, intrinsic dimensions, and modern formats reduce unnecessary image transfer while preserving quality.
Provide dimensions to prevent layout shifts and let the browser choose an appropriate source for the rendered size.
Pointer and hover capability
Touch, mouse, stylus, keyboard, and assistive technologies expose different interaction capabilities.
Do not hide essential actions behind hover and use capability media features only as enhancements rather than device identity checks.
Reduced motion
Some users request less animation because movement can cause discomfort or interfere with comprehension.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion and ensure state changes remain understandable when animation is minimized or removed.
Safe areas and mobile viewport
Display cutouts, browser chrome, and software keyboards can reduce the actually usable viewport.
Use safe-area environment variables and dynamic viewport units where full-height experiences genuinely require them.
Orientation and reflow
Landscape, portrait, split-screen, and resizable desktop windows can change available geometry at runtime.
Design reflow from available space rather than locking behavior to orientation assumptions.
Responsive verification
A responsive feature can appear correct at sampled widths while failing between them or with changed text size.
Test continuous resizing, zoom, long content, keyboard navigation, and representative real devices before release.

paths.title: Visual Design Systems, Typography & Tokens
paths.description: Translate visual intent into consistent tokens, typography, color, spacing, components, states, density, and theme behavior.
topics: Design tokens
Tokens give stable semantic names to recurring values such as surfaces, text, spacing, radius, and motion.
Prefer semantic tokens like --color-danger-text over component-specific raw values when multiple components share the meaning.
Typography hierarchy
Type size, weight, line height, measure, and spacing work together to communicate hierarchy and reading rhythm.
Define a limited type scale and test body text for readable line length, zoom behavior, and dense-content contexts.
Font loading
Web fonts can delay text or shift layout when fallback metrics differ from the final font.
Use a sensible font-display strategy, subset where appropriate, and tune fallback metrics when typography is layout-critical.
Color roles
Interface colors should map to semantic roles and preserve sufficient contrast across states and themes.
Define foreground/background pairs and verify normal, hover, focus, disabled, selected, success, warning, and error states.
Spacing system
A spacing scale reduces arbitrary one-off values and makes component relationships more predictable.
Choose a small scale, allow exceptions only for explicit reasons, and use gap when spacing belongs to a layout relationship.
Component variants
Variants should represent meaningful product states or sizes rather than every visual combination designers can imagine.
Keep a constrained variant API and compose primitives instead of creating a new variant for isolated screens.
Density modes
Data-heavy products may need compact and comfortable density while preserving hit targets and readability.
Change spacing and row height through tokens without shrinking interactive targets below accessible sizes.
Theme architecture
Light, dark, high-contrast, and branded themes should remap semantic tokens rather than duplicate whole component stylesheets.
Keep component rules theme-agnostic and override semantic token values at the theme boundary.
Motion language
Durations, easing, and spatial transitions should communicate relationship and state rather than decorate every interaction.
Use a small motion scale, respect reduced-motion preferences, and avoid animations that delay input or obscure final state.
Design-system governance
A component library becomes unreliable when product teams silently fork components or bypass tokens.
Document intended usage, test shared components, review breaking changes, and remove obsolete variants through explicit migrations.
codeExamples:
.prose { font-size:1rem; line-height:1.65; max-inline-size:68ch; }
.button { min-block-size:2.75rem; padding-inline:var(--space-4); border-radius:var(--radius-md); }

paths.title: JavaScript Language Fundamentals
paths.description: Understand values, scope, functions, objects, collections, modules, errors, equality, immutability, and language semantics used by frontend code.
topics: Primitive and object values
JavaScript primitives behave as values while objects and functions are referenced and can contain mutable state.
Know when an assignment copies a primitive versus shares an object reference, especially when updating UI state.
Lexical scope
let, const, functions, modules, and closures determine which bindings are visible at a point in code.
Use the narrowest useful scope and avoid implicit global state that couples unrelated features.
Functions as values
Functions can be passed, returned, stored, and closed over surrounding bindings.
Use callbacks and higher-order functions when they clarify data flow, not simply to compress code.
Object modeling
Objects group named properties and behavior, while prototypes define inheritance relationships behind many built-ins.
Prefer plain data shapes for transferable state and use classes or prototypes when shared behavior and lifecycle justify them.
Arrays and iteration
Array methods express mapping, filtering, searching, reducing, sorting, and transformation with different mutation behavior.
Choose the method whose semantics match the operation and avoid hidden quadratic work in hot rendering paths.
Equality and coercion
Strict equality avoids many implicit coercions, while Object.is and SameValueZero have specialized semantics.
Use explicit conversion at boundaries and prefer === for routine comparison unless a different equality model is required.
Nullish and optional access
null and undefined represent absence differently across APIs, and optional chaining short-circuits missing access.
Normalize external data deliberately and use ?? when valid falsy values such as 0 or empty strings must be preserved.
Destructuring and spread
Destructuring extracts values and spread creates shallow copies or merges iterable/object content.
Remember that spread is shallow and does not protect nested objects from shared mutation.
Modules
ES modules provide explicit imports, exports, dependency graphs, and per-module scope.
Use stable module boundaries and avoid circular dependencies that obscure initialization order.
Error semantics
throw, Error subclasses, try/catch/finally, and rejected promises represent failure paths that must remain observable.
Throw or return structured failures at clear boundaries and avoid catch blocks that silently convert defects into false success.

paths.title: DOM, Events & Browser APIs
paths.description: Manipulate documents safely through DOM APIs, event propagation, delegation, focus, observers, clipboard, workers, and browser capabilities.
topics: DOM querying
querySelector, getElementById, closest, matches, and collection APIs retrieve live or static document relationships.
Query from the narrowest stable root and cache references only when node lifetime makes that safe.
Safe DOM updates
textContent, createElement, attributes, classes, and structured DOM methods avoid interpreting untrusted strings as markup.
Use textContent for untrusted text and reserve innerHTML for trusted, reviewed markup with an explicit sanitization strategy.
Event propagation
Events travel through capture, target, and bubble phases and can be canceled when the event is cancelable.
Understand default behavior and propagation before calling preventDefault or stopPropagation.
Event delegation
A parent listener can handle events from dynamic descendants by inspecting the event target and closest matching ancestor.
Use delegation for large or changing lists while verifying that the matched element belongs to the intended container.
Focus management
Keyboard focus communicates where subsequent input will go and should follow logical interaction flow.
Move focus only when context changes require it, preserve visible focus, and return focus after temporary UI such as dialogs.
Mutation and resize observers
Observer APIs report DOM mutations or geometry changes asynchronously without constant polling.
Observe the narrowest target and disconnect observers when the component lifecycle ends.
IntersectionObserver
Intersection observation can detect visibility relative to a root for lazy work or analytics without manual scroll calculations.
Use it for noncritical visibility-driven behavior and do not equate intersection with actual user attention.
Clipboard and permissions
Clipboard, notifications, geolocation, and related APIs may require secure contexts, permission, or user activation.
Request powerful capabilities at the moment users understand why they are needed and handle denial as a normal state.
Web Workers
Workers execute JavaScript off the main thread with message-based communication and restricted DOM access.
Move isolated CPU-heavy tasks to a worker and keep transferred messages small enough that serialization does not erase the benefit.
Abortable browser work
AbortController can cancel fetches and many event/listener operations when UI context changes.
Create a controller per logical operation and abort stale requests during navigation, replacement, or component teardown.

paths.title: Async JavaScript, Fetch & Data States
paths.description: Model asynchronous work with promises, async functions, fetch, cancellation, concurrency, retries, caching, and explicit interface states.
topics: Promise states
A promise is pending until it fulfills with a value or rejects with a reason, and handlers create new promises.
Return or await promises consistently so callers can observe completion and failure rather than losing asynchronous errors.
Async functions
async functions always return promises and await pauses only that async function, not the entire JavaScript runtime.
Use await for readable dependency order and start independent operations before awaiting when concurrency is safe.
Fetch semantics
fetch rejects for network-level failure but normally resolves for HTTP error statuses such as 404 or 500.
Check response.ok or status explicitly before treating a response body as successful application data.
Response parsing
json(), text(), blob(), arrayBuffer(), and streams consume response bodies in different representations.
Choose parsing based on Content-Type and expected size, and handle malformed payloads separately from transport errors.
Loading state
Users need evidence that an operation is pending without losing context or triggering duplicate work.
Show a task-appropriate pending state, preserve useful existing content when possible, and disable only controls that truly conflict.
Empty and partial state
A successful request can legitimately return no items or incomplete optional information.
Design explicit empty, partial, stale, and unavailable states instead of rendering them as generic errors.
Request cancellation
Search, navigation, and rapidly changing filters can make older in-flight responses irrelevant.
Abort stale work or ignore results using stable request identity so late responses cannot overwrite newer state.
Concurrency control
Promise.all, allSettled, race, and any encode different relationships among concurrent operations.
Choose concurrency semantics based on whether every result is required, partial results are useful, or a timeout/first success matters.
Retry policy
Retries are safe only for suitable failure classes and operations that tolerate repetition.
Retry bounded transient failures with backoff and jitter, honor server guidance, and avoid automatically repeating unsafe mutations.
Client caching
Memory caches, HTTP caching, service workers, and application query caches solve different freshness and offline problems.
Define cache keys, freshness, invalidation, and stale behavior before adding a client cache abstraction.
